messages:
sylvia: Quick follow-up on the private networking RFC — we need to pick a long-term approach for control-plane connectivity into customer VPCs. Two contenders: an ephemeral reverse-connect "connector" that the customer runs (outbound-only), or regional private endpoints + peering per customer. New constraints: SOC wants KMS/HSM isolation for key material, Sales needs predictable egress IPs for customer allowlists, and a few regulated customers will require air-gapped/pull-only options. Thoughts?

kevin: Short take: connectors are simpler to operate at scale (no peering count, fewer route table ops). Downsides: connection churn, NAT/egress variability, and harder packet-level tracing.

maya: From a security/compliance POV, dedicated peering looks better — clearer traffic boundaries, VPC flow logs, and easier for some customers to audit. But peering per-customer scales poorly (route table explosion) and some clouds restrict cross-account peering.

tian: How about a hybrid pattern: regional private endpoint as primary for control-plane (stable route, static IPs), and lightweight connectors as an optional fallback for burst/air-gapped customers? Endpoint for policy/heartbeat, connector for heavy KV/cache warmups or telemetry.

alex: One question: who terminates TLS? If customers insist on managing certs, we should support mTLS with per-customer client certs that they control (rotate via KMS). That reduces trust surface for private endpoint.

rebecca: Edge case: certain financial customers ban peering and any inbound network. For them the only viable model is a pull-only connector that originates to Redwood and uses the control plane channel to fetch config. Keep that in mind.

infra-bot: deploy-bot: connector-v2 rollout scheduled to staging on 2024-04-01 03:00 UTC. Watch logs in #eng-oncall.

sylvia: Concrete list of tradeoffs I want recorded in the RFC follow-up: operational blast radius, cost per-tenant (peers vs NAT egress), latency for initial handshake/warm cache, observability/span propagation across connector vs peering, upgrade/rollback story, and customer on-boarding friction.

kevin: I'll draft a compact tradeoff table tomorrow with rough cost numbers. Quick placeholder — NAT egress unpredictability is the main blocker for customers who whitelist IPs. For canary, suggest migrating 10 customers to connectors first, measure failures, then expand.

maya: Also call out billing implications: static IPs enable per-customer firewall billing and smoother enterprise sales. Connectors can be made stable only if we provide managed NAT pools on our side (not great), or instruct customers to set up their own NAT with static IPs.

tian: Implementation notes if we pick private endpoints: need route propagation support, per-tenant route tagging in the control plane, and a cert distribution flow. I can prototype a CSR->signed cert flow using SSM Parameter Store + signed CSR where customer approves via console.

alex: I'll mock up the mTLS rotation flow and the minimal API surface: `POST /tenant/{id}/csr -> signed cert`, background rotation webhook. Also include KMS-backed signing to avoid persisting private keys on our control plane.

sylvia: OK — action items: @kevin draft tradeoff table + estimated monthly cost model, @maya enumerate security/compliance constraints and a matrix of customers who must have peering vs connectors, @tian prototype cert/CSR flow, @alex mock mTLS rotation API. I'll synthesize into RFC follow-up and propose decision criteria.

kevin: ack. I'll add a tiny ASCII diagram in the doc tomorrow to show path differences and a sample curl for the CSR flow.

kevin: ```
Customer VPC (connector) ---> outbound TLS ---> Redwood connector pool ---> control plane
Customer VPC (peering) <--- private endpoint (static IP) ---> control plane
```

sylvia: Thanks all — let's close the loop in 48h. If anyone has hard blockers call them out now. :thumbsup:
